newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish officials differ over privatisation list.
newsitem.headline: Polish officials differ over privatisation list.

text.p: Polish government officials appeared to be at odds on Wednesday over a list of large state-owned firms, shares of which are to be sold to finance a crucial reform of the country's ailing social security system.

The cabinet minister in charge of the reform, Jerzy Hausner, wants to have the list ready quickly, while the treasury minister, preparing the list, is in no hurry to present it, Hausner and his top aide said on Wednesday.
"We would like this list to be created as soon as possible... Work on the list is carried out in the treasury ministry," Michal Rutkowski, director of Hausner's office, told a news conference.

Hausner later told Reuters that Treasury Minister Miroslaw Pietrewicz, known to share his Peasant party's generally cautious attitude towards privatisation, was reluctant to quickly unveil the list because this might arouse controversy. @

"I can't tell you when the list will be ready. In my view if we had the list, this would give the (pension reform) programme a higher profile, but the minister (Pietrewicz) thinks there is still time for this," Hausner said.
"The minister thinks this (the list) might result in disquiet," he said without elaborating.
Neither Pietrewicz nor his spokesman was immediately available to comment.
Since the fall of communism in 1989, privatisation has always been a political minefield, notably at election time. @

The current campaign for parliamentary polls, scheduled around September, is no exception, with the opposition Solidarity Electoral Action (AWS) stepping up its criticism of the pension reform and privatisation plans of the government coalition of ex-communists and the Peasant party.

Under the government's pension reform scheme, the finance ministry is to issue bonds, convertible into shares of the companies from the list, if the national budget cannot bear the costs of the reform in any other way.

The costs stemming from the creation of new pension funds, are estimated at about one percent of Poland's gross domestic product annually for more than 20 years from the date of the reform's launch, possibly in 1999.
GDP is forecast at 430 billion zlotys in 1997.

Government officials have said that the list of companies -- which is to be appended to three pension reform bills due to be discussed by parliament on Thursday -- would be made up of 60-70 firms with good financial results.

A statement by Hausner's office, issued on Wednesday, confirmed that the list was likely to include such large firms as copper combine KGHM Polska Miedz SA, telecoms monopoly TPSA, Bank Handlowy SA, farming bank BGZ SA, air carrier LOT SA, fuels distributor CPN SA, the Plock oil refinery, gas and oil firm PGNiG and tourism agency Orbis SA.
Rutkowski said it would be up to the government to decide each year how much of these companies would be sold, either directly or through convertible bonds, to finance the reform.
